narrative: During the 2020s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture continue to thrive, building upon decades of rich tradition and self-expression. The natural hair movement, which originated in the 1960s and resurged in popularity in the 2000s, remains a powerful force, encouraging individuals to celebrate their afro-textured hair in all its glory. Styles like the Afro, Cornrows, Bantu knots, and Box braids are staples of African hair culture, each with its own unique history and significance. Dreadlocks, also known as locs, have become increasingly popular, allowing wearers to showcase their individuality while embracing a natural, carefree aesthetic. Protective hairstyles, designed to minimize manipulation and environmental damage, remain essential for maintaining healthy hair. While the Jheri curl, a popular style of the 1980s and early 1990s, has largely faded from mainstream culture, its legacy lives on in the continued celebration of Black women's beauty and identity through their hairstyles. Despite limited documentation on this specific decade, it is clear that Black and African women's hair culture remains a vibrant and integral part of their identities, reflecting a deep connection to tradition, community, and self-expression.
